questions.stem: In Australia's national workplace relations system, a modern award is:
options: a written contract agreed privately between an individual employee and an employer
a bonus paid to employees who exceed productivity targets set by their employer
a document setting minimum pay rates and conditions for an industry or occupation
an agreement negotiated between one employer and its own employees and their union
questions.explanation: Modern awards, made and varied by the Fair Work Commission, set minimum wages and conditions across an industry or occupation. A workplace-level deal is an enterprise agreement, and a private deal is an individual contract.

questions.stem: The independent body that sets the national minimum wage and modern award rates under the Fair Work Act 2009 is:
options: the Australian Bureau of Statistics
the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission
the Fair Work Commission
the Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: The Fair Work Commission, Australia's national workplace relations tribunal, conducts the Annual Wage Review and makes and varies modern awards. The Fair Work Ombudsman enforces compliance.

questions.stem: An enterprise bargaining agreement is:
options: a decision of the Fair Work Commission raising the national minimum wage each year
a collective agreement on pay and conditions made at the level of a business or workplace
a set of minimum pay rates that applies to every worker in a particular industry
a contract under which a worker supplies services to a business as a contractor
questions.explanation: Enterprise agreements are negotiated between an employer and its employees, often represented by a union, and approved by the Fair Work Commission. They replace the award for the employees they cover.

questions.stem: Before the Fair Work Commission approves an enterprise agreement, the agreement must generally pass the better off overall test (BOOT). This test checks that:
options: employees would be better off overall than under the relevant modern award
the employer's profits would be higher overall than under the relevant award
every single term is more generous than the matching term in the award
employees would earn more than the average wage in their industry overall
questions.explanation: The BOOT compares the agreement as a whole with the award, so a less generous term can be offset by a more generous one. It protects the award as a floor rather than requiring every term to be better.

questions.stem: Under the Fair Work Act 2009, employees can take protected industrial action, such as a strike, mainly:
options: only when the Fair Work Commission has refused to raise the national minimum wage
whenever an individual employee disagrees with a direction given by their manager
while bargaining for a proposed enterprise agreement, after a protected action ballot
at any time during the life of an approved enterprise agreement, without notice
questions.explanation: Industrial action is protected only during bargaining for a new agreement and after employees have voted for it in a ballot. Action during the life of an approved agreement is not protected.

questions.stem: A highly skilled engineer negotiates her own salary, well above the award rate, directly with her employer. This wage-setting mechanism is:
options: an industry award
the national minimum wage
an individual arrangement
an enterprise bargaining agreement
questions.explanation: Individual arrangements, usually common law contracts, are agreed between one employee and the employer. They must at least meet the National Employment Standards and any award or agreement that applies.

questions.stem: Which statement about individual arrangements in Australia is correct?
options: They are set each year by the Fair Work Commission in its wage review
They cannot provide less than the minimum entitlements in the safety net
They allow employers to pay below the national minimum wage if workers agree
They must be approved by a ballot of all employees at the workplace
questions.explanation: An individual contract can add to, but not undercut, the National Employment Standards and the minimum wage. Ballots apply to enterprise agreements, and the Annual Wage Review sets minimums rather than individual pay.

questions.stem: Which group of workers is most likely to be paid exactly the award rate?
options: Professionals with specialised skills that are in short supply
Public servants covered by a large enterprise agreement
Low-paid workers in industries such as hospitality and retail
Senior managers in large mining and finance companies
questions.explanation: Award reliance is highest among low-paid workers with little bargaining power, often in hospitality, retail and care work. Skilled and senior workers usually earn above the award through agreements or individual contracts.

questions.stem: Centralised wage determination means that:
options: wages are negotiated mainly between employers and employees at each workplace
wages are set mainly by market forces without any minimum or award rates
wages are fixed by each state government for the workers in that state
wages are set mainly by a central tribunal and flow on across industries
questions.explanation: Under a centralised system a body such as the industrial tribunal sets wage increases that apply broadly. Workplace bargaining is the decentralised approach.

questions.stem: Since the early 1990s, Australia's wage-setting system has become:
options: controlled by the Reserve Bank, which sets wages alongside the cash rate
more decentralised, with enterprise bargaining now central to wage-setting
more centralised, with national wage cases setting nearly every worker's pay
fully deregulated, with awards and the minimum wage abolished entirely
questions.explanation: Enterprise bargaining was introduced in the early 1990s and expanded through later reforms, shifting wage-setting towards the workplace. A safety net of awards and the minimum wage remains.

questions.stem: An advantage of decentralised wage determination is that:
options: low-skilled workers gain greater bargaining power relative to employers
industrial disputes become impossible because no bargaining takes place
wages can be linked to productivity and conditions in each business
all workers in the same occupation receive the same increase each year
questions.explanation: Bargaining at the workplace lets pay reflect a firm's productivity, profitability and needs, which can improve efficiency and flexibility. It tends to weaken, not strengthen, the position of low-skilled workers.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of decentralised wage determination is that it can:
options: prevent wages from reflecting differences in productivity between firms
make wages inflexible, as one central decision applies to all workers
remove any link between a business's profitability and its wage costs
widen wage inequality, as workers with little bargaining power fall behind
questions.explanation: Workers with scarce skills or strong unions can win large rises, while low-skilled workers struggle to bargain, so pay gaps widen. Inflexibility and weak links to productivity are criticisms of centralised systems.

questions.stem: An advantage claimed for centralised wage determination is that it:
options: allows each business to tailor pay closely to its own productivity
encourages workers to bargain directly with their own employer
lets wages in booming industries rise faster than in other sectors
delivers fairer outcomes and can restrain wage growth across the economy
questions.explanation: A central tribunal can deliver consistent increases, protect lower-paid workers and help keep wage growth in line with inflation targets, as under the Prices and Incomes Accord of the 1980s. Tailoring pay to each firm is a feature of decentralisation.

questions.stem: During a resources boom, wages for mine workers rise rapidly. Under a highly centralised system with strong flow-on, a key risk would be that:
options: the Fair Work Commission loses its power to set award minimum wages for all industries
large rises spread to all industries regardless of productivity, adding to inflation
mine workers' wages fall behind those in other industries as rises are held back
wages in industries outside mining become more flexible than wages in mining
questions.explanation: With strong flow-on, a rise won in one booming sector can be passed to workers everywhere, including where productivity has not grown, pushing up costs and prices. Decentralisation confines such rises to the sector concerned.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a non-standard work arrangement?
options: A permanent role with set weekly hours
An ongoing salaried position with super
Casual employment with irregular hours
A permanent full-time job with paid leave
questions.explanation: Non-standard work includes casual, fixed-term, labour hire and gig work, and contracting. A permanent full-time job with leave entitlements is the standard arrangement it is compared against.

questions.stem: Casual employees under most modern awards receive a casual loading, commonly 25%, mainly to compensate them for:
options: being ineligible for superannuation contributions from their employer
having no paid annual leave or personal leave and less job security
working longer hours each week than permanent full-time employees
paying a higher rate of income tax than permanent employees do
questions.explanation: The loading is paid instead of entitlements such as paid annual and personal leave that permanent staff receive. Casual employees are still entitled to superannuation guarantee contributions.

questions.stem: A benefit of non-standard work arrangements for businesses is:
options: lower hourly wage costs, as casual rates are below permanent rates
the flexibility to adjust staff numbers and hours as demand changes
lower turnover and stronger loyalty among their employees over time
higher training investment, as workers stay with the firm for longer
questions.explanation: Casual and contract staff let firms match labour to busy and quiet periods. Casual hourly rates usually include a loading, and insecure work tends to raise turnover and reduce training.

questions.stem: A cost of non-standard work for individuals is:
options: a legal ban on working for more than one employer at the same time
irregular income that can make it harder to obtain a home loan
less freedom to choose when and how many hours they work
loss of the national minimum wage and all award protections
questions.explanation: Unpredictable hours and income make budgeting and borrowing harder. Casual and part-time employees remain covered by the minimum wage and awards, and many value the flexibility.

questions.stem: Gig economy platforms such as food delivery apps often engage workers as independent contractors rather than employees. The main economic concern is that these workers may:
options: pay no income tax on the earnings they receive from the platform
fall outside parts of the safety net, such as award rates and paid leave
earn more than the national minimum wage for each hour they spend working
be forced to work fixed shifts set by the platform each week
questions.explanation: Contractors have not traditionally been covered by awards, the minimum wage or leave entitlements, raising concerns about low effective pay and insecurity. Gig work usually offers flexible, not fixed, hours.

questions.stem: For the economy as a whole, a benefit of non-standard work arrangements is that they can:
options: remove the need for any safety net of minimum pay and conditions
raise participation by people who cannot work standard full-time hours
raise productivity by increasing the training firms give casual staff
lower underemployment, as all part-time workers want fewer hours of work
questions.explanation: Flexible arrangements let students, carers and older workers take part in the labour force. Many part-time workers want more hours, which is why underemployment is a concern.

questions.stem: Australia's industrial safety net consists mainly of:
options: the National Employment Standards, modern awards and the national minimum wage
enterprise agreements, individual contracts and employee share schemes
the age pension, JobSeeker Payment and Commonwealth Rent Assistance
the cash rate, the inflation target and the exchange rate of the dollar
questions.explanation: These set the minimum pay and conditions below which employment terms cannot fall. Welfare payments are part of the social security system, not the industrial safety net.

questions.stem: Which is one of the National Employment Standards for full-time employees?
options: A guaranteed annual pay rise of 5%
Twelve weeks of paid annual leave each year
A guaranteed bonus tied to company profits
Four weeks of paid annual leave each year
questions.explanation: The National Employment Standards include four weeks of paid annual leave, ten days of paid personal and carer's leave and maximum weekly hours of 38 plus reasonable additional hours. They do not guarantee pay rises or bonuses.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the national minimum wage is to:
options: protect low-paid workers and provide a fair floor under pay
keep inflation inside the Reserve Bank's target band
raise the profits of small businesses with few employees
set the pay of senior managers in Australia's large listed companies
questions.explanation: The minimum wage ensures the lowest-paid employees receive a fair, relevant minimum and protects them from exploitation. Inflation is managed mainly through monetary policy.

questions.stem: In its Annual Wage Review the Fair Work Commission must balance several considerations. Which pair best shows the trade-off it faces?
options: Raising the living standards of the low paid versus the risk of reducing employment
Lowering the exchange rate versus raising the terms of trade for exporters
Raising company tax revenue versus reducing government welfare spending
Increasing house prices versus increasing the rate of population growth
questions.explanation: A higher minimum wage improves the incomes of low-paid workers but raises labour costs, which may lead some employers to hire fewer people or cut hours. The Commission also weighs productivity, inflation and the needs of business.

questions.stem: A large rise in the minimum wage, well above productivity growth, is most likely to:
options: reduce the incomes of low-paid workers who keep their jobs after the increase
raise firms' labour costs and could add to inflation or reduce hiring of low-skilled workers
lower firms' labour costs and lead them to hire more low-skilled workers over time
have no effect on prices, as minimum wages apply only to public sector workers
questions.explanation: When wages rise faster than productivity, unit labour costs increase, so firms may raise prices or employ fewer low-skilled workers. Workers who keep their jobs gain higher incomes.

questions.stem: The proportion of Australian employees who are trade union members has:
options: risen from about 13% in the early 1990s to around 40% by the mid-2020s
stayed close to 40% of all employees in every year since the early 1990s
fallen to zero since enterprise bargaining replaced the award system
fallen from about 40% in the early 1990s to around 13% by the mid-2020s
questions.explanation: ABS data show union membership falling from about 40% of employees in 1992 to around 13% in 2024. The decline reflects structural change, more non-standard work and changes in workplace laws.

questions.stem: Falling union representation is most likely to affect wage outcomes by:
options: raising the national minimum wage, which unions no longer need to argue for
ending enterprise bargaining, which can be done only by registered unions
reducing employees' collective bargaining power, which can slow wage growth
increasing employees' bargaining power, which can speed up wage growth
questions.explanation: Unions bargain collectively on behalf of members, so lower membership weakens workers' bargaining position, one factor economists cite in slow wage growth. Enterprise bargaining can occur without a union.

questions.stem: Which factor has contributed to the long-term decline in union membership in Australia?
options: A sharp rise in the share of workers employed in the public sector
Growth of service and casual jobs, in which unions have traditionally been weaker
Growth of manufacturing employment, in which unions have traditionally been weaker
Laws making union membership compulsory for all workers in large businesses
questions.explanation: Employment has shifted from heavily unionised manufacturing towards services and casual work, where membership is low. Compulsory unionism was removed, not introduced, and the public sector remains among the most unionised.

questions.stem: An economist argues that stronger unions could raise wages but might also have costs. Which is the most likely cost?
options: Lower prices for consumers as businesses compete for unionised workers
Fewer industrial disputes as workers lose the right to bargain collectively
Wage rises above productivity growth that raise unemployment in some industries
Wage cuts below productivity growth that reduce consumer spending sharply
questions.explanation: If unions win increases faster than productivity, labour costs rise and some employers may hire fewer workers. Stronger unions are associated with more, not fewer, disputes and with higher wages.

questions.stem: Which is a role of trade unions in Australian wage-setting?
options: Approving enterprise agreements under the better off overall test
Enforcing award rates by issuing fines to employers who underpay
Bargaining for enterprise agreements on behalf of their members
Setting the national minimum wage in the Annual Wage Review
questions.explanation: Unions act as bargaining representatives in enterprise bargaining and make submissions to the Annual Wage Review. The Fair Work Commission sets the minimum wage and approves agreements, and the Fair Work Ombudsman enforces compliance.

questions.stem: Government funding for fee-free TAFE places in areas of skill shortage aims mainly to:
options: raise the skills of the workforce and reduce structural unemployment
lower the cash rate by reducing the demand for credit from students
reduce frictional unemployment by speeding up job advertising online
lower the participation rate by keeping young people out of work
questions.explanation: Training matches workers' skills to the jobs available, which reduces structural unemployment and lifts productivity. Frictional unemployment is about the time taken to move between jobs.

questions.stem: Skilled migration policy can improve the size and skills of Australia's workforce, but a limitation is that:
options: it cannot be changed once a migration program has been set
it can reduce employers' incentive to train local workers
it always lowers wages for every Australian-born worker
it reduces the working-age share of the population
questions.explanation: Easy access to skilled migrants may lead firms to recruit from overseas rather than invest in training. Migration tends to raise the working-age share, and program levels are reviewed each year.

questions.stem: A limitation of education and training as a labour market policy is:
options: the long lag before graduates enter the workforce with new skills
the immediate rise in unemployment as students leave their jobs
the loss of any effect on productivity once training is complete
the legal requirement to fully fund every course chosen by students
questions.explanation: Courses take years to complete, so skill shortages identified today may persist, or change, before trainees are ready. This policy lag limits how quickly training can respond.

questions.stem: A government proposes major changes to workplace laws, but the changes are watered down after strong opposition from both business groups and unions. This illustrates which limitation of labour market policy?
options: policy lags
global free riders
the zero lower bound on rates
political considerations
questions.explanation: Labour market reform affects powerful interest groups, so political pressure can limit or reverse it. Policy lags are delays in recognising problems and in policies taking effect.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would best suggest that labour market policies are helping to achieve full employment?
options: A falling unemployment rate alongside fewer reported skill shortages
A rising unemployment rate alongside more reported skill shortages
A rising underemployment rate as more part-time workers want hours
A falling participation rate as more people stop looking for work
questions.explanation: Lower unemployment with fewer skill shortages suggests workers' skills are better matched to available jobs. A falling participation rate can reflect discouraged workers rather than success.
